transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-12-22
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Aisha Patel (Redwood AE), Evan Liu (Redwood SE), Marcus Lee (CTO, Orion HealthTech), Sofia Ramirez (Lead ML Engineer), Daniel Cho (Security Architect)

Summary: Quick discovery call. Orion currently on OpenAI plus some on-prem vLLM for latency-sensitive paths. They're evaluating Redwood Dedicated or Private for cost predictability, data controls, and eval parity. Main asks: how close Redwood models are to OpenAI outputs, migration complexity for prompts and tooling, benchmarks for latency/cost, and security/KMS/VPC requirements.

Topics: migration path from OpenAI, vLLM/TGI compatibility, eval parity, Dedicated sizing, SOC2/KMS/VPC, benchmarks and next steps.

[00:00] Aisha: Hey everyone, thanks for taking time today. Quick intros? I'm Aisha, account lead at Redwood. Evan is our systems engineer who will handle the technical bits.
[00:18] Marcus: Hi everyone, Marcus here. CTO at Orion HealthTech. We run clinical summarization pipelines and are currently heavy OpenAI usage, cost's getting out of hand.
[00:28] Sofia: Sofia, ML lead. We also have an internal vLLM deployment for low-latency endpoints right now. Want to see if Redwood Dedicated can replace both.
[00:37] Daniel: Daniel, security. I'll focus on compliance, KMS, and network isolation.
[00:45] Evan: Great, thanks. Quick agenda: confirm current stack, goals for migration, blockers, and outline a benchmark plan.

[03:12] Marcus: Our current stack: primary generation on OpenAI GPT-4o early access. Some latency-critical inference on vLLM running weights (GGML-ish) inside our cluster. We also use TGI for a couple models. Main drivers: cost and control. We need parity on outputs for our regulatory evals.
[03:45] Aisha: When you say parity, do you mean exact token-level parity or just evaluation metrics like ROUGE/clinical accuracy?
[03:53] Sofia: Good q. We need eval parity on our turn-by-turn clinical grading tests. Slight wording differences are ok but not changes that affect clinical decision signals.
[04:10] Evan: Understood. On parity, we typically see variation vs OpenAI because model weights and tokenizers differ. For open models we provide Redwood-verified variants and recommendations on quantization and tokenization to get close. For blackbox OpenAI models the approach is about behavioral parity via prompt engineering and ensemble fallbacks.
[04:35] Marcus: So you can run the same model weights as OpenAI?
[04:40] Evan: Not for OpenAI-proprietary models. For their weights we can't host the exact proprietary weights. But for many workflows teams have migrated to open weights that approximate behavior, or we run Redwood-hosted tuned variants. We also support function-calling and streaming semantics similar to OpenAI to reduce app changes.
[05:05] Marcus: That is a risk for us. Our compliance evals were done against GPT-4o outputs. If we move away we need a clear validation plan.
[05:15] Aisha: Totally. That's why we propose a two-step pilot: benchmarking parity on your evals and a small Dedicated cluster for a canary. Evan, can you talk about the bench?
[05:24] Evan: Sure. We run a side-by-side experiment: you provide sample prompts and labels, we run them against your OpenAI baseline and the Redwood-hosted dedicated stack, track metrics (ROUGE, hallucination rate, safety flags), plus latency p50/p95 and cost per 1k tokens. For vLLM/TGI endpoints we can also replay logs to compare runtime behavior.
[05:50] Sofia: How do you handle tokenizer differences? We saw tokenization mismatch when switching from OpenAI to Eleuther-based tokenizers.
[06:00] Evan: Two options: we can normalize tokenization at the client side, or we recommend a model variant whose tokenizer aligns. We also include a small pre-processing shim to map prompt templates to tokenization that preserves your evaluation metrics. It's usually part of the bench setup.
[06:18] Daniel: Security: do you support KMS and bring-your-own-key? We need to ensure keys are customer-controlled for Private deployment and at rest encryption for Dedicated.
[06:28] Evan: Yes. Dedicated supports KMS integrations and customer-managed keys for storage encryption. Private offering (VPC/on-prem) gives you full control. For Hosted we have envelope encryption and we can offer additional controls under enterprise contracts.
[06:45] Daniel: And SOC2/ISO? Audit logs?
[06:50] Aisha: We have SOC2 Type II, ISO 27001 in our security pack, and per-request audit logs available in Redwood Console. We'll send the security whitepaper and SOC2 artifacts as follow-up.

[09:00] Marcus: Can you share expected latency numbers? Right now vLLM endpoints give us p50 around 30ms for short prompts, OpenAI about 100-200ms.
[09:12] Evan: Short story: Dedicated on modern GPUs can get sub-100ms p50 for optimized models and request patterns, but it depends on batch sizing and kv cache warmness. For production DED setups we tune batching and continuous KV cache to hit your latency SLOs. If you need 30ms we might recommend a hybrid: a small Dedicated hot-path or Private co-located inference on specialized hardware.
[09:40] Sofia: What about streaming and function calling? We rely on streaming responses and function calling heavily.
[09:46] Evan: We support streaming, tool calling, and structured output. We also have function-calling compatibility layers that mimic OpenAI semantics. There are edge cases where payload sizes and callback ordering differ slightly; we'll validate those in the bench.

[12:30] Marcus: Cost model: how predictable is Dedicated? We don't want surprise spikes.
[12:38] Aisha: Dedicated is reserved capacity with predictable monthly commitments. You can configure burst capacity too. We give per-route cost breakdowns and Redwood Console shows token-level cost. We can model your current usage to suggest a plan.
[12:55] Marcus: Ok. Another question: how invasive is the integration? We have SDKs built for OpenAI API calls, webhooks, and infra automation.
[13:05] Evan: We provide a compatible REST/SDK surface, and often integration is minimal: swap endpoints and keys. For Private, network setup (VPC peering, routing) takes more work. We'll also help with rollout strategies: canary, A/B, and automatic fallback to hosted OpenAI during the pilot if needed.
[13:32] Sofia: Any customers who moved from OpenAI with similar regulatory constraints?
[13:37] Aisha: Yes, a couple of healthcare SaaS customers. We'll anonymize and share a short case study focusing on benchmark approach and rollout.

[16:00] Marcus: About eval parity again — suppose we run the bench and see worse RF1/clinical metrics, what levers do we have?
[16:08] Evan: Levers: try different model weights, adjust quantization levels, apply RLHF style tuning if allowed, change prompt templates, or keep specific flows on OpenAI while migrating the rest. The Redwood Optimize tool will recommend quant and batching settings to trade off cost/latency without big regressions.
[16:36] Daniel: For compliance, do you keep logs? Are logs encrypted and can we control retention?
[16:42] Evan: Logs are stored in the Console. Retention and access controls can be configured; audit logs can be forwarded to your SIEM. All stored logs respect encryption at rest and KMS settings.

[19:20] Sofia: We also use TGI for some experimental models. Will Redwood work with that stack?
[19:26] Evan: We can ingest model artifacts in multiple formats; we support model conversions and can run your TGI models if licensing allows. Compatibility varies; we usually do a quick model onboarding to confirm.
[19:45] Marcus: Do you support vLLM style batching/serve patterns?
[19:50] Evan: Our runtime supports continuous batching and KV cache management similar to vLLM, and for Dedicated we provide kernel and compilation optimizations to get better throughput.

[22:00] Aisha: Any questions on SLAs, uptime?
[22:04] Daniel: Yes, SLA numbers for Dedicated and Hosted, and incident escalation.
[22:10] Aisha: Dedicated has SLA-backed uptime targets; we'll include SLA terms in the follow-up. For enterprise deals we include dedicated support contacts and escalation paths.

[25:00] Evan: For the benchmark, we'll need: sample prompt set, expected labels, a replay of production logs if possible, and one week of typical traffic pattern. We'll run OpenAI baseline (if you can share call records or run locally) and then Redwood Dedicated.
[25:25] Marcus: We cannot share OpenAI call logs easily due to ToS, but we can run the OpenAI baseline on our side and share outputs.
[25:32] Evan: That's fine; having reference outputs works. If you can share the prompts and expected metrics, we can run the Redwood side and compare.

[28:10] Sofia: How long to stand up a Dedicated test cluster?
[28:14] Evan: For a pilot we can provision a small Dedicated pool within 2-3 weeks once contract and infra access are in place. Private on-prem takes longer due to networking and hardware procurement.

[31:00] Marcus: Any blockers on our side we should know?
[31:05] Evan: We'll need access to sample datasets, a list of critical endpoints, and a technical contact to help with any model artifacts. Also firewall rules if you want VPC peering.

[33:40] Daniel: Legal: data residency and DPA. We need a DPA and clarity on subprocessors.
[33:47] Aisha: We'll share our standard DPA and a list of subprocessors. For Private deployments we can limit subprocessors per contract.

[36:00] Marcus: Let's talk migration timeline. We aim to start pilot in Jan and roll to prod in Q1 if bench is good. Is that realistic?
[36:10] Evan: Yes, pilot in early Jan is feasible. Bench and validation usually takes 2-4 weeks depending on dataset and pass/fail criteria. Production rollout depends on bench results but Q1 launch is an achievable target.

[38:50] Sofia: Any gotchas with prompts that use advanced function calling and streaming? We've had issues with partial object serialization switching between providers.
[38:58] Evan: We'll validate those exact prompts in bench. In a few cases serialization order differs; we can provide a compatibility shim or adopt Redwood's structured output schema. Usually it's a small integration change.

[41:20] Marcus: If we decide to keep some flows on OpenAI and others on Redwood, is routing supported?
[41:26] Evan: Yes, Smart routing by policy is supported. You can route by latency, cost, region, or even by confidence thresholds and fall back to a different model if needed.

[44:00] Daniel: For encryption keys, if we use BYOK, how does key rotation work?
[44:05] Evan: We support KMS rotation policies. For Dedicated we can coordinate rotation windows so there is no downtime. We'll include docs in the security pack.

[46:30] Aisha: To summarize next steps: we'll send pricing and a Dedicated sizing worksheet; Evan will draft the bench plan and request list; Marcus will provide prompts and sample data access; Daniel will confirm required compliance docs.
[46:50] Marcus: Sounds good. A couple of dates: can we aim to receive pricing by Dec 24 and schedule the bench setup call in the week of Jan 5?
[47:00] Aisha: Yes we can do that. Evan, you'll own the bench setup?
[47:05] Evan: Yep. I'll follow up with a bench plan and calendar invite.

[49:20] Sofia: One more: do you support per-route cost analytics so we can attribute tokens to product features?
[49:26] Aisha: Redwood Console has token-level cost breakdowns per route and model. We'll show a quick example in the follow-up deck.

[51:00] Marcus: Thanks everyone. If bench shows parity and cost is right, we're likely to move ahead with Dedicated.
[51:10] Aisha: Great, appreciate the time. We'll follow up with the documents and calendar invites.
[51:20] Daniel: Thank you.
[51:25] End of meeting

References shared during call: pricing worksheet link (sent after), security whitepaper link (will send), benchmark plan doc (Evan to send).
